polynomial-end-behavior-s1.title: The graph of a polynomial function $q$

plot.label: Graph of q(x) = -0.1(x + 3)(x + 1)(x - 2)(x - 4): both ends fall; it has two high points at about (-2.2, 2.5) and (3.2, 2.5) and zeros at -3, -1, 2 and 4

table.caption: Values of p(x) = 2x^3 - 50x^2 at large inputs x

items.q: The graph shows $q(x) = -0.1(x + 3)(x + 1)(x - 2)(x - 4)$. Which describes the right end of the graph?
options: $\lim_{x \to \infty} q(x) = \infty$
$\lim_{x \to \infty} q(x) = -\infty$
$\lim_{x \to \infty} q(x) = 0$
$\lim_{x \to -\infty} q(x) = -\infty$

why.correct: The leading term is $-0.1x^4$: for large $x$, $x^4$ is huge and positive, and $-0.1$ makes it huge and negative. So $\lim_{x \to \infty} q(x) = -\infty$.
options: The right end falls, so the outputs decrease without bound.
Right: as $x$ increases without bound, $q(x)$ decreases without bound.
The graph does not level off at $0$; it keeps falling.
This is about the left end, $x \to -\infty$.

items.q: The graph shows $q(x) = -0.1(x + 3)(x + 1)(x - 2)(x - 4)$. Which describes the left end of the graph?
options: $\lim_{x \to -\infty} q(x) = \infty$
$\lim_{x \to -\infty} q(x) = -3$
$\lim_{x \to -\infty} q(x) = -\infty$
$\lim_{x \to \infty} q(x) = -\infty$

why.correct: $-0.1x^4$ is negative for every large $|x|$, so both ends fall: $\lim_{x \to -\infty} q(x) = -\infty$.
options: For even degree, both ends go the same way; here both fall.
$-3$ is a zero; the graph keeps falling past it.
Right: $(-x)^4 = x^4$ is positive, times $-0.1$, so the outputs fall without bound.
True, but that describes the right end.

items.q: The graph shows $q(x) = -0.1(x + 3)(x + 1)(x - 2)(x - 4)$. What are the degree and the sign of the leading coefficient of $q$?
options: Degree $4$, negative
Degree $4$, positive
Degree $3$, negative
Degree $5$, negative

why.correct: Leading term $-0.1 \cdot x \cdot x \cdot x \cdot x = -0.1x^4$: even degree (ends match) and negative (both fall).
options: Right: four factors of $x$, and the leading coefficient is $-0.1$.
A positive leading coefficient with even degree would make both ends rise.
Odd degree would send the two ends in opposite directions.
There are four factors $(x - a)$: degree $4$.

items.q: The graph shows $q(x) = -0.1(x + 3)(x + 1)(x - 2)(x - 4)$. Which statement about $q$ on all real numbers is supported by its end behavior?
options: $q$ has a global minimum but no global maximum.
$q$ has a global maximum but no global minimum.
$q$ has both a global maximum and a global minimum.
$q$ has neither a global maximum nor a global minimum.

why.correct: $\lim_{x \to \pm\infty} q(x) = -\infty$: the graph comes up from the bottom on the left and goes back down on the right, so it has a highest point but no lowest.
options: Both ends fall without bound, so there is no lowest output.
Right: both ends fall, so the outputs have a highest value (about $2.5$) but no lowest.
Outputs that fall without bound have no least value.
An even-degree polynomial has one or the other; here, a global maximum.

items.q: The graph shows $q(x) = -0.1(x + 3)(x + 1)(x - 2)(x - 4)$. Which leading term gives the same end behavior as $q$?

why.correct: End behavior depends only on the degree's parity and the leading coefficient's sign. Even and negative: both ends fall, like $-0.1x^4$ or $-2x^6$.
options: Both ends of $0.1x^4$ rise.
For odd degree the left end of $-0.1x^3$ rises.
Right: even degree and a negative coefficient, so both ends fall, as for $q$.
For odd degree the ends go opposite ways.

items.q: The table gives values of $p(x) = 2x^3 - 50x^2$. Which statement describes the end behavior of $p$ as $x$ increases?
options: $\lim_{x \to \infty} p(x) = -\infty$
$\lim_{x \to \infty} p(x) = 1500000$
$\lim_{x \to \infty} p(x) = \infty$
$\lim_{x \to \infty} p(x) = 2$

why.correct: For large $x$ the leading term $2x^3$ is far bigger than $50x^2$, so $p(x)$ grows without bound: $\lim_{x \to \infty} p(x) = \infty$.
options: The first values are negative, but by $x = 30$ the outputs grow without bound.
$1{,}500{,}000$ is one output; the outputs keep growing.
Right: the leading term $2x^3$ wins for large $x$.
$2$ is the leading coefficient, not a limit of the outputs.

items.q: The table gives values of $p(x) = 2x^3 - 50x^2$. Why are $p(10)$ and $p(20)$ negative even though $p(x)$ grows without bound?
options: $-50x^2$ is larger in size than $2x^3$ until $x$ passes $25$.
The table's values were computed incorrectly from the formula.
So the end behavior is really $\lim_{x \to \infty} p(x) = -\infty$.
Negative outputs mean the leading coefficient is negative.

why.correct: End behavior is about large inputs. $p(x) = 2x^2(x - 25)$ is negative for $0 < x < 25$ and positive after, so the leading term takes over only past $x = 25$.
options: Right: $2x^3 > 50x^2$ exactly when $x > 25$; after that the leading term dominates.
The later values grow without bound; the end behavior is about large $x$.
The leading coefficient, $2$, is positive.

items.q: The table gives values of $p(x) = 2x^3 - 50x^2$. Which describes $p$ as $x$ decreases without bound?
options: $\lim_{x \to -\infty} p(x) = \infty$
$\lim_{x \to -\infty} p(x) = -\infty$
$\lim_{x \to -\infty} p(x) = 0$
$\lim_{x \to -\infty} p(x) = -50$

why.correct: For large negative $x$, $2x^3$ is huge and negative and dominates $-50x^2$: $\lim_{x \to -\infty} p(x) = -\infty$.
options: $2x^3$ is negative for negative $x$, so the left end falls.
Right: for odd degree with a positive leading coefficient, the left end falls.
The outputs do not level off; $2x^3$ grows without bound in size.
$-50$ is a coefficient, not an output the graph approaches.

items.q: The table gives values of $p(x) = 2x^3 - 50x^2$. What is the largest zero of $p$?

mistakes.why: $0$ is a zero (a double one), but $p(x) = 2x^2(x - 25)$ has a larger one.

why.correct: $2x^3 - 50x^2 = 2x^2(x - 25)$, so the zeros are $0$ and $25$. That is where $p$ turns from negative to positive.

items.q: What is the leading term of $f(x) = (2x - 1)^3(x + 4)$?

mistakes.why: Cube the whole leading part of $(2x - 1)$: $(2x)^3 = 8x^3$.
Multiply by the $x$ from $(x + 4)$ too: $8x^3 \cdot x = 8x^4$.

why.correct: Multiply the leading parts of the factors: $(2x)^3 \cdot x = 8x^3 \cdot x = 8x^4$. So $f$ has degree $4$, leading coefficient $8$, and both ends rise.

options: $\lim_{x \to -\infty} g(x) = -\infty$
$\lim_{x \to -\infty} g(x) = -3$
$\lim_{x \to -\infty} g(x) = 100$
$\lim_{x \to -\infty} g(x) = \infty$

why.correct: For large $|x|$ the leading term $-3x^5$ dominates. If $x$ is negative, $x^5$ is negative and $-3x^5$ is positive: $\lim_{x \to -\infty} g(x) = \infty$.
options: $-3x^5$ is positive for negative $x$: a negative times a negative.
$-3$ is the leading coefficient, not a value the outputs approach.
The coefficients do not give the limit; the leading term does.
Right: the leading term $-3x^5$ is positive and huge for large negative $x$.

items.q: For which functions do both $\lim_{x \to \infty} f(x) = -\infty$ and $\lim_{x \to -\infty} f(x) = -\infty$ hold? Select all that apply.

why.correct: Both ends fall exactly when the degree is even and the leading coefficient is negative.
options: Yes: even degree, negative leading coefficient.
Yes: even degree, negative leading coefficient.
No: odd degree, so the ends go opposite ways.
No: its left end rises, $\lim_{x \to -\infty} (-x^3) = \infty$.

items.q: Which statement about $\lim_{x \to \infty} f(x)$ for $f(x) = x^2$ is written correctly?
options: $f \to \infty$
$\lim_{x \to \infty} f(x) = \infty$
$f(\infty) = \infty$
$\lim_{x \to \infty} f(x) \to \infty$

why.correct: Write limit notation in full: $\lim_{x \to \infty} f(x) = \infty$. Graders do not accept "$f \to \infty$" or $f(\infty)$.
options: It leaves out the input: say $x \to \infty$, in limit notation.
Right: function, input, where the input goes, and where the outputs go.
$\infty$ is not an input; $f(\infty)$ means nothing.
Do not mix an arrow into the statement: the limit equals $\infty$.

items.q: Why must a polynomial function of odd degree have at least one real zero?
options: Its ends go in opposite directions, so the graph must cross the $x$-axis.
Its leading coefficient is positive.
It has exactly as many real zeros as its degree, counting each one.
Its graph always passes through the origin.

why.correct: For odd degree, $\lim_{x \to \infty} f(x)$ and $\lim_{x \to -\infty} f(x)$ have opposite signs ($\pm\infty$). A polynomial's graph is unbroken, so it crosses the $x$-axis somewhere in between.
options: Right: one end is below the axis and the other above, and the graph has no breaks.
The argument works for negative leading coefficients too.
Some zeros may be non-real; $x^3 + x$ has only one real zero.
Many do not: $x^3 + 1$ has odd degree, but its graph meets the $y$-axis at $1$, and its real zero is $x = -1$.

items.q: What is $\lim_{x \to \infty} h(x)$ for $h(x) = x^2(3 - x)^3$?
options: $\infty$
$-\infty$

why.correct: Multiply the leading parts: $x^2 \cdot (-x)^3 = -x^5$. Odd degree, negative coefficient: $\lim_{x \to \infty} h(x) = -\infty$.
options: $(3 - x)^3$ has leading part $(-x)^3 = -x^3$, which is negative.
$27$ is the leading part of $3^3$, not the behavior for large $x$.
The outputs grow in size; they do not shrink to $0$.
Right: the leading term is $x^2 \cdot (-x)^3 = -x^5$.

items.q: Let $f(x) = 0.01x^4$ and $g(x) = 1000x^3$. Which statement about large positive values of $x$ is true?
options: $g(x) > f(x)$ for large $x$, because its coefficient is far larger
$f(x) > g(x)$ once $x > 100{,}000$, because the higher degree wins
$f(x) = g(x)$ for large $x$, because both have the limit $\infty$
$g(x) > f(x)$ for large $x$, because $x^3$ grows faster than $x^4$

why.correct: $\frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \frac{0.01x^4}{1000x^3} = \frac{x}{100{,}000}$, which is greater than $1$ when $x > 100{,}000$ and keeps growing. As $x$ increases without bound, the term of higher degree dominates, whatever the coefficients are.
options: The coefficient gives $g$ a head start, but $\frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \frac{x}{100{,}000}$ passes $1$ at $x = 100{,}000$.
The ratio $\frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \frac{x}{100{,}000}$ exceeds $1$ from there on.
Both grow without bound, but not at the same pace: their ratio $\frac{x}{100{,}000}$ keeps growing.
For $x > 1$, $x^4$ is larger than $x^3$: a higher power grows faster.
